Problem Solving by Search

Uninformed and Informed Search Algorithms

The heart of the course. How an agent that does not know the answer can still find it — first blindly, then with a sense of direction.

Search is a fundamental concept in Computer Science. In Artificial Intelligence, we use search to explore possible actions and find solutions to problems. In this module, you will learn how to turn a real-world problem into a search problem, explore possible solutions, and compare different search strategies. We will focus on understanding the ideas through simple examples and practical activities, rather than memorizing many algorithms.

Learning objectives

  • Model the problem: explain why a goal-based agent needs search, and formulate a real-world problem as a search problem — initial state, actions, transition model, goal test, and action cost.
  • Model the problem: tell a state from a node and the state space from the search tree, and follow how the frontier grows as nodes are expanded.
  • Explain the strategy: judge a search strategy on completeness, optimality, time, and memory, without confusing search time with path cost.
  • Explain the strategy: explain how BFS, DFS, and UCS choose the next node, tell them apart, and say when each one is suitable.
  • Experiment and compare: trace greedy best-first search and A* on a small map, computing g, h, and f, and compare the paths they return.
  • Explain the strategy: decide whether a heuristic is admissible, and explain why that matters for A*.
  • Experiment and compare: test search strategies on the same problem, explain the results, and choose a strategy for a new problem.
i
How this module is organized
  • Core — learn and apply: problem formulation (3.1); state, node, search tree, and frontier (3.2); evaluating strategies (3.3); greedy best-first search, A*, and admissible heuristics (3.5–3.6).
  • Review — refresh what you know: BFS, DFS, and UCS from Computer Science (3.4).
  • Further exploration — optional: DLS and IDS (3.4); heuristic dominance and heuristic design (3.6). These topics are outside the module quiz.

Key terms in this module

Search problem
A problem described by five parts: initial state, actions, transition model, goal test, and action cost.
State space
Every state that can be reached from the initial state, joined by the actions that move between them. It is produced by the five parts; think of it as the map.
Solution
Any path from the initial state to a goal. An optimal solution is a cheapest one.
Abstraction
Keeping the information needed to solve the problem, and leaving out details that do not affect the answer.
Search tree
The record of the search: a root node for the initial state, and a child node for each action tried. One state can appear in many nodes.
State
A description of a situation in the problem, such as In(C): the driver is at C.
Node
A search record in the search tree: a state, plus how it was reached — the node it came from, the action taken, and the path cost so far. Several nodes may represent the same state.
Frontier
The nodes waiting to be expanded: created, but not expanded yet. A queue in BFS, a stack in DFS, a priority queue in UCS and A*. It is not the reached table.
Reached table
The states the search has reached so far, each with the best node found for it. BFS skips a state already in the table; UCS and A* replace the entry when they find a cheaper path.
Expand
To apply every legal action to a node's state and create its child nodes.
Tree-like search
Search that keeps no reached table, so the same state can appear in many nodes and be expanded again on every path that reaches it.
Graph search
Search that keeps a reached table, so it does not explore the same state again unless it finds a cheaper path to it. Tree-like search keeps no such table.
Branching factor, b
How many actions are available at a typical state. With d, the depth of the shallowest goal, and m, the deepest level, it measures the time and memory of a search.
Path cost, g(n)
The total cost of the steps taken from the start up to node n. It is a property of the answer, not of the work the algorithm did.
Time complexity, space complexity
How much work a search algorithm does (counted as nodes created or expanded) and how much it must store at once (nodes in memory). Not the same as the path cost of its answer.
Complete
The algorithm finds a solution whenever one exists — under stated conditions, such as a finite branching factor.
Optimal
The algorithm finds a cheapest solution, not just any solution. Also called cost-optimal.
Uninformed search
Also called blind search. It uses only the five parts of the problem, so it cannot tell which state is closer to the goal.
BFS say: Breadth-First Search
Expands the shallowest node first, using a queue. Finds the path with the fewest steps.
UCS say: Uniform-Cost Search
Expands the node with the lowest path cost g(n) first, using a priority queue. The same idea as Dijkstra's algorithm, stopped when the goal is taken out.
DFS say: Depth-First Search
Expands the deepest node first, using a stack. Tree-like DFS needs very little memory, but it guarantees neither a solution nor the cheapest one.
DLS say: Depth-Limited Search
Optional reading. DFS that refuses to go deeper than a fixed limit.
IDS say: Iterative Deepening Search
Optional reading. Runs DLS again and again with a limit of 0, 1, 2, 3... until the goal is found. Not the same as IDA*, which this course does not cover.
Informed search
Search that uses extra knowledge, usually a heuristic h(n), to decide which node to expand next.
Heuristic, h(n) say: hyoo-RIS-tik
An estimate of the cost still remaining from node n to the goal. It uses available knowledge about the problem and does not have to be exact. It is not one of the five parts of the problem.
Straight-line distance
The distance between two places in a straight line. On a road map it is never longer than the real road, so it is an admissible heuristic when the cost is distance.
Greedy best-first search
Expands the node with the smallest h(n) and ignores the cost already paid. It can be fast, but it is not optimal.
A* say: A-star
The main algorithm of this module. It expands the node with the smallest f(n) = g(n) + h(n): what you already paid, plus what you still expect to pay. The star is part of the name, not a multiplication sign — see section 3.5.
Admissible
A heuristic that never overestimates the real remaining cost. It is the condition that makes A* return a cheapest path, when the branching factor is finite, every step costs at least some ε > 0, and cheaper paths found later are handled correctly.
Consistent
A stronger condition: one step can never improve the estimate by more than that step costs, h(n) ≤ c + h(n'). Every consistent heuristic is also admissible.
Misplaced tiles, h₁
Optional reading. An 8-puzzle heuristic: the number of tiles that are not in their correct square.
Manhattan distance, h₂
Optional reading. An 8-puzzle heuristic: for every tile, its horizontal plus vertical distance from its correct square, added up.
Dominance
Optional reading. h₂ dominates h₁ if both are admissible and h₂(n) ≥ h₁(n) for every node. A* with h₂ then usually expands fewer nodes; the exact guarantee is in section 3.6.
Relaxed problem
Optional reading. The same problem with some rules removed, so it is easier to solve exactly. Its exact cost is an admissible heuristic for the real problem.
Section 3.1

Why AI Needs Search and Problem Formulation

What does it mean to search for a solution?

You have met search before. In a data structures course you search an array for a number, a file for a word, or a database for a student record. The thing you want is already stored, and the search finds it.

In AI, search has the same purpose: find what we need. But what we look for is different. We usually look for a way to reach a goal: a sequence of actions, such as the roads that take a driver to a customer. Some problems keep all their possibilities in memory, like a small map. In others there are too many to store, so the next possibilities are worked out from a few rules, one step at a time. If you have met BFS and DFS on graphs, they are the same algorithms you will use in section 3.4.

The delivery driver's questions

Imagine you deliver for a pizza shop, or for DHL, SMSA or Aramex, and you have several orders to deliver this morning. Before you start the car, you have to answer three questions:

  • Which customer do you visit first?
  • How do you compare two possible routes?
  • What information do you need before you decide?

Different people answer in different ways. But every answer uses the same ingredients: places, the roads between them, distances, a rule for when the job is done, and a way to compare one route with another. That list is the start of a search problem.

Why does artificial intelligence need search?

In Module 2 we met the goal-based agent: it knows what it wants. Knowing the goal is not the same as knowing how to reach it. A delivery app knows the customer's address, but it does not know in advance which sequence of roads reaches that address at the lowest cost — and with a new order every few minutes, nobody can write those sequences for it beforehand. A simple reflex agent would need a condition–action rule for every situation it could meet.

Search solves this differently. The agent tries possible action sequences in a model of the world, before it takes any of them in the real world. It explores possibilities in an order set by a strategy, and it remembers what it has already tried. Some strategies also use an estimate of the remaining cost to decide what to try next (section 3.5).

Search and AI are closely connected in two ways: search helps AI solve problems, while knowledge and intelligent methods can guide search towards promising solutions.

AI and search: two complementary relationships

Search supports AI

Search helps AI agents plan actions, solve problems, and find useful solutions or configurations.

Intelligence guides search

Knowledge, heuristics, and learned models can help search focus on promising possibilities instead of exploring everything.

Steps 2 and 3 happen inside the agent, before it moves. Only the sequence found in step 4 is carried out in the world.
Driving from Makkah to Jeddah: without a map, and with one

Without a map, you reach a junction, pick a road, and find out by driving. You are exploring the real world, and every wrong turn costs real kilometres.

With a map, you try the roads on paper first, choose a route, and only then drive. This module is about the second way: the agent searches in its model of the world, and then acts.

This module works in the setting described in section 2.4 — fully observable, deterministic, static, discrete, single-agent — and sequential, because a plan is a sequence of actions. So the agent can plan the whole route before it takes the first step, and then follow it. If the world surprises it — a road is closed — it perceives the change and searches again, as maps apps do when traffic changes (section 3.7).

The five parts of a search problem

To learn the ideas, we start with one order and one customer, and we use this small example for the rest of the module. A restaurant, S, must send an order to a customer, G. The driver can pass through four other places, A, B, C and D. The numbers on the roads are kilometres, and every road can be driven in both directions.

A map shows the places and roads, but it does not fully describe the problem to an AI agent. The agent also needs to know where to start, what moves are possible, where each move leads, when the goal is reached, and how much each move costs. These are the five parts of a search problem. They are components of one description, not steps that the agent carries out in order.

  1. Initial state

    Where the agent starts: In(S), the driver is at the restaurant.

  2. Actions

    What the agent can do in a state. In In(S): drive to A, drive to B, or drive to D. The actions depend on the state: from D, the only road leads back to S.

  3. Transition model

    Where each action leads: RESULT(In(S), Go(A)) = In(A).

  4. Goal test

    A check that answers "am I done?" Here it is one state, In(G). Sometimes it is a condition instead, such as "every exam has a time slot, and no student has two exams at the same time".

  5. Action cost

    What one step costs: here, the kilometres of the road. Add the costs along a path and you get the path cost. The action cost can reflect part of the performance measure from Module 2, such as distance or time, but it is not the whole measure.

Any solution, or the best solution?

A solution is any path from the initial state to a goal. On the delivery map, S → B → G is a solution: it reaches the customer, and it costs 2 + 7 = 9 km. S → A → C → G is also a solution, and it costs 3 + 2 + 3 = 8 km. The first reaches the goal; the second is cheaper.

An optimal solution is a solution with the lowest path cost. "Optimal" is always measured against the action costs we chose. Here the cost is distance in kilometres, so S → A → C → G is optimal. If the cost were travel time, the optimal route could be a different one.

Not every problem asks for the cheapest solution. Sometimes any path to the goal is enough; sometimes we want a cheapest one, such as the shortest route to the customer. Sections 3.3 and 3.4 show which algorithms promise a cheapest solution.

Abstraction: keeping what matters

In our delivery model, we keep the places, roads, and distances because they affect the route. We leave out details such as the driver's name and the colour of the vehicle because they do not affect the answer in this simplified problem. This is called abstraction: keeping the information needed to solve the problem. In a real delivery service, details such as traffic, vehicle capacity, or delivery time windows may matter too; then a good formulation includes them. You will use abstraction in every module of this course.

Notice what is not among the five parts: a heuristic. A heuristic is extra knowledge that some search algorithms use, such as an estimate of how far the goal is (section 3.5). It is not one of the five components of a search problem: the problem is complete without it.

A good formulation comes first

Before an AI agent can search for a solution, we must describe the problem clearly. A good formulation identifies what matters, what actions are possible, and what counts as success. If the problem is described incorrectly, even a good search algorithm may produce the wrong answer.

i
Further exploration: the 8-puzzle (not in the quiz)

The 8-puzzle is a classic search problem: a 3×3 frame with eight numbered tiles and one empty square. A tile next to the empty square can slide into it. The goal is to put the tiles in order.

Two moves solve this example: slide tile 5 up, then tile 8 left.

The five parts. States: which tile is in which square. Initial state: a given arrangement. Actions: move the empty square left, right, up, or down (describing one empty square is easier than describing eight tiles). Transition model: the empty square swaps with the tile next to it. Goal test: the tiles are in the goal arrangement. Action cost: 1 per move.

Not every arrangement can be solved. The tiles can be arranged in 9! = 362,880 ways, but sliding moves can never change a certain parity property of the arrangement. So only half of the arrangements, 181,440, can reach a given goal; from the other half, no sequence of moves reaches it. Even 181,440 states are far too many to draw: a search algorithm discovers them one at a time.

Optional: the five parts in Python

In code, all five parts fit in one small class. Every problem in this module plugs into it:

class Problem:
    """The five parts of a search problem."""

    def __init__(self, initial, goal=None):
        self.initial = initial          # 1. where we start
        self.goal = goal

    def actions(self, state):           # 2. what can I do here?
        raise NotImplementedError

    def result(self, state, action):    # 3. where does it take me?
        raise NotImplementedError

    def is_goal(self, state):           # 4. am I done?
        return state == self.goal

    def action_cost(self, s, action, s_next):   # 5. what did it cost?
        return 1
Check yourself

Back to the driver's morning: three customers, X, Y and Z, instead of one. The driver must visit all three, in any order. With one customer, a state was just the driver's place, such as In(A). Is that enough now? If not, what else must a state record? And what is the goal test?

Show answer

The place is not enough. Standing at Y after serving X is a different situation from standing at Y with nobody served yet. A state must record where the driver is and which customers have already been served, for example In(Y), served {X, Y}.

Goal test: all three customers are served. The actions and costs stay the same: drive along a road and pay its kilometres.

With many customers, choosing the best order is close to a famous hard problem, the travelling salesman problem (TSP). Module 4 returns to this problem, where the quality of the final route matters more than the path the search took to find it.

Now that we know how to describe a search problem, we can explore what happens when a search algorithm starts working on it.

Section 3.2

State Spaces, Search Trees, and Frontiers

The five parts of section 3.1 are a description that you write. This section looks at what that description produces, and at what a search algorithm builds while it works.

The state space is every state that can be reached from the initial state, joined by the actions that move between them. It is fixed before the search starts. The delivery map is small enough to draw its state space: six places and seven roads. Many problems have far too many states to draw, so a search algorithm discovers them one at a time.

The state space is the map of the world. The search tree is the record of your walk through it. They are not the same thing, and the difference matters in every algorithm that follows.

Walking the alleys of Al-Balad in Jeddah with a notebook

The old district has a fixed layout: small squares joined by narrow alleys. That layout is the state space. It exists whether you walk it or not.

Your notebook is the search tree: "from the gate I went right, then left, then hit a closed alley; back at the gate I went left..." The same small square can appear on three pages of your notebook, because you reached it three different ways. One place, three notes.

A state describes a situation in the problem: In(C), the driver is at C. A node is a search record that contains a state and information about how it was reached: the node it came from, the action taken, and the path cost so far. Some programs also store its depth: the number of steps from the start. Several nodes may represent the same state, because several paths can lead to it.

بالعربية

الحالة (State) وصفٌ لموقف في المسألة، مثل وجود السائق عند C. أما العقدة (Node) فسجلٌّ تكتبه خوارزمية البحث: يحوي حالةً، ومعها الطريق الذي أوصل إليها وتكلفته. لذلك قد تظهر الحالة الواحدة في أكثر من عقدة.

Watching a search grow

A search starts with one node, for the initial state. To expand a node means to apply every legal action to its state and create its child nodes. A node is created (textbooks also say generated) when its parent is expanded. The nodes and the links between them form the search tree.

Frontier — nodes waiting to be expanded. Imagine exploring a map. You have already explored some places, and you have discovered other places that you have not explored yet.

The frontier holds the search nodes waiting to be expanded: they have been created, but not expanded yet. The algorithm takes a node out of the frontier, expands it, and adds new nodes when appropriate.

بالعربية

الـFrontier هي قائمة انتظار للعُقد التي اكتشفتها خوارزمية البحث، لكنها لم توسّعها بعد لمعرفة ما يمكن الوصول إليه منها.

Here is the start of a search on the delivery map. We expand three nodes: S, then A, then B. This is a tree-like search illustration, without repeated-state elimination: every path that reaches a place makes a new node. The order is only an illustration. It is not the result of any particular algorithm: choosing which node to expand next is exactly what the algorithms in section 3.4 do differently.

StepExpandNew nodes createdFrontier after the step
0—S (the start)S
1SA, B, DA, B, D
2AS, CB, D, S, C
3BS, C, GD, S, C, S, C, G
Tree-like search illustration, without repeated-state elimination. Each expansion takes one node out of the frontier and adds its children. The last column lists the waiting nodes; it does not show the order in which an algorithm would choose them.
The map does not change. The tree grows with every expansion, and the same place can appear in many nodes.

Two kinds of node are now in the tree. After three expansions, 9 nodes have been created: the 3 we expanded, and 6 still waiting in the frontier. In short: frontier = discovered nodes waiting to be expanded.

Before a node is created, it is not discovered: nothing in the tree stands for it yet. So every node moves through the same three stages, always in this order. Follow node A through steps 0, 1 and 2 of the table above:

Dotted: not discovered — no node created yet. Dashed: in the frontier — created, not expanded. Filled: expanded — taken out of the frontier, children created. The explorer in section 3.4 uses the same three looks.

Now look at the states inside those nodes. S appears three times and C twice, although the map has only six places. Every path that reaches a place makes a new node. That is the repeated-state problem, and we return to it below.

The repeated-state problem

If the map has a cycle, the search tree can be infinite even though the map has only six places: S → A → S → A → ... forever. Two common ways to handle it: tree-like search does not check whether a state has been reached before; graph search keeps a reached table.

The reached table records each state the search has reached, with the best node found for it so far. It is not the frontier: the frontier holds nodes still waiting to be expanded, while the reached table remembers states, including those whose nodes have already been expanded.

Tree-like search

Remember nothing

  • Needs no table of visited states
  • Can loop forever: a two-way road is already a cycle, S → A → S → A ...
  • Repeats the same work many times
  • Fine only when no state can be reached in two ways
Graph search

Keep a reached table

  • Records every state reached, with the best node found for it
  • Stops on a finite state space, because each state is expanded a limited number of times
  • Costs memory: one entry per state reached
  • The default choice in this course

What happens when graph search reaches a state that is already in the reached table? It depends on the algorithm. BFS simply skips it: the first path BFS finds to a state has the fewest steps. UCS and A* compare costs: if the new path is cheaper, they replace the entry in the table and put the new node in the frontier (sections 3.4 and 3.5).

On the delivery map, graph search makes the same three expansions much smaller. When A is expanded, S is already in the reached table with cost 0, so the new S (cost 6) is not added; C is new, so it is added with cost 5. When B is expanded, S (cost 4) is skipped again. C through B would cost 6, more than the 5 already recorded, so it is skipped too. G is new and is added with cost 9. The frontier holds D, C and G: three nodes instead of six.

How search works: the frontier loop

Search algorithms use the same general process, but differ mainly in how they choose the next node from the frontier and how they handle repeated states. Here is the shared process:

  1. Start with a frontier

    The frontier holds nodes that have been created but not expanded yet. At the start it holds only the node for the initial state.

  2. Take one node out of the frontier

    This is the main difference between algorithms. Which node you take — the oldest, the newest, the cheapest, the most promising — decides whether you are running BFS, DFS, UCS, or A*.

  3. Test it

    If it is a goal, follow the parent links back to the start and return the path. (BFS can safely test earlier, when a node is created — see its code in section 3.4.)

  4. Expand it

    Create its children: apply every legal action, and add the new nodes to the frontier. In graph search, a child whose state is already in the reached table is usually skipped; the exact rule depends on the algorithm, as described above.

  5. Repeat

    Until you find a goal, or the frontier is empty — which means there is no solution. On a very large or infinite state space, the loop may run for a very long time, or never end (section 3.3).

The frontier is not an algorithm. It is the list of waiting nodes; the algorithm is the rule that chooses which node leaves it. The reached table is a different thing again: it remembers states, including states whose nodes have already been expanded.

Optional: nodes and expansion in Python 
class Node:
    def __init__(self, state, parent=None, action=None, path_cost=0):
        self.state, self.parent = state, parent
        self.action, self.path_cost = action, path_cost

def expand(problem, node):
    """Make the child nodes — one for every legal action."""
    for action in problem.actions(node.state):
        s_next = problem.result(node.state, action)
        cost = node.path_cost + problem.action_cost(node.state, action, s_next)
        yield Node(s_next, parent=node, action=action, path_cost=cost)

def path(node):
    """Follow the parent links back to the start, then reverse."""
    steps = []
    while node.parent is not None:
        steps.append(node.action)
        node = node.parent
    return list(reversed(steps))
Check yourself

A map has 6 places. You run a tree-like search and your search tree now holds 40 nodes. Is something broken?

Show answer

No, this is normal. Without a reached table, the same place is created again on every path that leads to it, so nodes are many more than states. It wastes work, but the answer is still correct. BFS with a reached table would expand at most 6 nodes, one per state. UCS and A* may add a place again when they find a cheaper path to it, but the table still stops the endless repeats.

Section 3.3

Evaluating Search Algorithms

Two search algorithms may both find a route to the same destination — or one of them may find none at all. Even when both succeed, they may differ in the cost of the route, the work needed to find it, and the memory they use. How can we compare them?

We ask the same four questions about every algorithm in the rest of this course:

✅ Complete?

If a solution exists, will the algorithm always find it?

🏆 Optimal?

Does it find the cheapest solution, or just any solution?

⏱️ Time complexity

How much work does it do? We count the nodes it creates (or expands) before it finishes.

💾 Space complexity

How much memory does it need? We count the nodes it must hold at the same time.

The dispatcher and the driver

At a delivery company, a dispatcher plans each route on a whiteboard, and then a driver drives it. The algorithm is the dispatcher, not the driver. Complete: whenever a route exists, the dispatcher finds one. Optimal: the route found is a shortest one. Time: how many partial routes the dispatcher writes down and checks before answering. Memory: how many partial routes must stay on the whiteboard at the same time.

A dispatcher who always finds the shortest route is still useless if the whiteboard is full before the answer comes.

Do not mixWhat it measuresDelivery example
Path costthe answer: the cost of the solution paththe 8 km the driver will drive
Search timethe algorithm's work: nodes created or expandedthe partial routes the dispatcher checked
Search memorywhat the algorithm stores while it works: the frontier and the reached tablethe partial routes on the whiteboard at once
The driving distance says nothing about how long the dispatcher took to find it.

Counting the nodes an algorithm creates or expands measures its computational work. It is not the same as the time on a clock: the same count can take less time on a fast computer and more on a slow one. Counting nodes lets us compare algorithms fairly, whatever machine runs them.

Why does search become expensive so quickly?

Every state offers several actions, and every action leads to a new state that offers several more. So the number of possible paths is multiplied again at every level of the search tree. Three letters describe this growth:

b — the branching factor: how many actions are available at a typical state. d — the depth of the nearest goal. m — the deepest the tree can go, which may be infinite. We write costs using these letters: $O(b^d)$, $O(b^m)$, $O(bd)$.

How fast is that growth in real numbers? Take $b = 10$, one microsecond to make a node, and 100 bytes to store it:

One microsecond and 100 bytes per node, counting only the bd nodes of the deepest level. Rounded numbers: the shape is the lesson, not the digits.

Even a small increase in search depth can create an enormous number of possibilities. This is one reason why choosing an efficient search strategy matters. A good strategy, or a good heuristic (section 3.5), can often reduce the number of nodes a search creates. In general, it does not remove this exponential growth.

Memory fails first

Look at depth 12 again. Waiting 12 days is painful but possible. Finding 100 terabytes of RAM is not. With these numbers, an algorithm that needs exponential memory fails long before one that needs exponential time. This is why the memory column matters as much as the time column when you compare algorithms.

!
When do we test for the goal?

Some books test a node when it is created. Others test it when it is taken out of the frontier. Testing on creation is faster, but it can return a path that is not the cheapest, because a cheaper path to the same goal may still be waiting in the frontier. Safe rule for UCS and A*: test when you take the node out, not when you put it in.

You will see this rule at work twice: in UCS (section 3.4), and in the A* worked example (section 3.5), where a goal node with cost 9 enters the frontier first, but the search goes on and returns the 8 km route. BFS is the exception: when every step costs the same, it can safely test a node when it is created (section 3.4).

Section 3.4

Uninformed Search

Breadth-First, Depth-First, and Uniform-Cost Search

How do search strategies differ?

We now know how to define a search problem and how a search algorithm explores states. But when several nodes are waiting in the frontier, which one should the algorithm explore next?

Different search strategies answer this question in different ways. Some use only the information in the problem itself. Others use extra knowledge, such as an estimate of the remaining cost to the goal.

Uninformed search

Uses the problem definition without a heuristic estimate of the remaining cost.

Examples: BFS, DFS, UCS (this section).

Informed search

Uses additional knowledge, usually a heuristic, to help choose which nodes to explore.

Examples: greedy best-first search, A* (section 3.5).

The three uninformed algorithms differ in how they choose the next node from the frontier:

  • BFS → the shallowest node first
  • DFS → the deepest node first
  • UCS → the lowest path cost first

Uninformed search is also called blind search: it knows nothing except the five parts of the problem, so it cannot tell which state looks closer to the goal. This section is a review — you may already know BFS and DFS from graphs in data structures. For each one, learn how it chooses the next node, what it guarantees, and when to use it. Detailed tracing practice comes with greedy search and A* in section 3.5.

Looking for one office inside a large building

Breadth-first: check every office on floor 1, then every office on floor 2, then floor 3. You will find the nearest office first, but you must remember every door you have not opened yet.

Depth-first: walk down one corridor, take every turn you meet, until you reach a dead end. Then step back and try the next door. You need almost no memory, but you may wander into the basement while your office is next to the entrance.

1. Breadth-First Search (BFS)

Rule: take out the shallowest node — the one created earliest. Frontier: a FIFO queue, first in, first out.

BFS can test a node for the goal as soon as it is created, because the first goal it creates is always a shallowest one. That gives a path with the fewest steps. The fewest steps is also the lowest path cost only when every step costs the same.

Optional: BFS in Python 
from collections import deque

def breadth_first_search(problem):
    node = Node(problem.initial)
    if problem.is_goal(node.state):
        return node
    frontier = deque([node])            # queue: oldest node leaves first
    reached = {problem.initial}
    while frontier:
        node = frontier.popleft()
        for child in expand(problem, node):
            if problem.is_goal(child.state):
                return child            # fewest steps (cheapest if costs are equal)
            if child.state not in reached:
                reached.add(child.state)
                frontier.append(child)
    return None                         # no solution

On the delivery map, BFS returns S → B → G: two roads, the fewest possible, but 9 km.

Result: complete when the branching factor $b$ is finite. Guaranteed to be optimal when every step costs the same — on the delivery map S → A → C → G is only 8 km. Time and memory are both $O(b^d)$. The memory is what hurts most: BFS must hold a whole level of the tree at once.

Use it when all steps cost the same and there is enough memory.

2. Depth-First Search (DFS)

Rule: take out the deepest node — the one created most recently. Frontier: a LIFO stack, last in, first out.

The strong point of DFS is memory. In its tree-like form it remembers only the current path and the unexpanded siblings along it: $O(bm)$ instead of $O(b^d)$. If the deepest path has 12 steps ($m = 12$) and $b = 10$, that is about 120 nodes, where BFS at the same depth may need a trillion. The saving disappears if DFS keeps a reached table of every state it has reached: the table can grow to the size of the whole state space.

Result: no general guarantee of a cheapest path, or even of the fewest steps. Completeness depends on the search space and on how repeated states are handled. Tree-like DFS is not complete: it can go around a cycle forever. If it checks the current path for repeated states, it is complete in a finite state space — but in an infinite one it can still follow an endless branch. Time $O(b^m)$; memory $O(bm)$ for tree-like DFS.

Use it when memory is tight, any solution will do, and the state space is finite and not too deep.

Explore: BFS and DFS on the same tree

The two rules give very different orders. Choose an algorithm, then press Next step or Play; Previous goes back one expansion. Watch which node comes out of the frontier each time. Run both to the end to see a short comparison.

3. Uniform-Cost Search (UCS)

Rule: UCS takes out the frontier node with the lowest accumulated path cost, g(n). Frontier: a priority queue ordered by $g$. It is the same idea as Dijkstra's algorithm, stopped as soon as the goal is taken out.

BFS counts steps. UCS counts cost. On the delivery map, the action cost is distance in kilometres, and the roads have different lengths. So the path with the fewest roads is not always the shortest, and UCS becomes the right tool.

On the delivery map, UCS takes out S (0), then B (2), then A (3) and D (3), then C (5), and finally G (8). Along the way it creates G with $g = 9$ when it expands B — but it does not stop there. It returns S → A → C → G, 8 km, where BFS returned S → B → G, 9 km.

UCS compares the total cost from the start, not just the cost of the next road. After it expands B, the cheapest road out of B is B–C, 4 km. But UCS does not follow it. It takes out A next, because $g(A) = 3$ is the lowest path cost in the frontier.

i
Why UCS must test the goal when it takes the node out

Finding a goal node inside the frontier only proves that a path exists. It does not prove it is the cheapest. Only when that node reaches the front of the queue do you know that nothing cheaper is left.

Result: complete and optimal, provided $b$ is finite and every step costs at least some fixed amount $\varepsilon > 0$.

Use it when steps have different costs, you need a cheapest path, and you have no heuristic.

Optional: UCS with very small step costs

If step costs can shrink towards zero, UCS can spend forever on ever-cheaper steps. Its time and memory depend on $C^*/\varepsilon$ — the cost of the best solution divided by the smallest step cost — and are written $O(b^{1+\lfloor C^*/\varepsilon \rfloor})$. With many tiny steps it can be much slower than BFS.

DLS and IDS are in the further exploration box below.
i
Further exploration: limiting the depth (not in the quiz)

Depth-limited search (DLS) is DFS with a fixed limit: it never goes deeper than $\ell$ levels. This stops an endless branch, but if the goal is deeper than the limit, DLS never finds it: it is complete only if $\ell \ge d$, and it is not optimal. Its time is $O(b^{\ell})$ and its memory $O(b\ell)$. Sometimes the problem gives a safe limit: on a map with 20 cities, no sensible route uses more than 19 roads.

Iterative deepening search (IDS) runs DLS with limit 0, then 1, then 2, and so on, until it finds the goal. It repeats the top levels, but they are small. With $b = 10$ and the goal at depth 5, IDS creates about 11% more nodes than BFS (123,450 against 111,110), yet it keeps about 50 nodes in memory instead of 100,000. Like BFS, it is complete when $b$ is finite and optimal when all steps cost the same, and its time is $O(b^d)$; like DFS, it needs only $O(bd)$ memory. That makes it a good choice when steps cost the same, memory is tight, and the depth of the goal is unknown.

Check yourself

A robot moves around a warehouse in Riyadh. Moving to the next cell takes 1 second, but passing through a narrow aisle takes 4 seconds. You want the fastest route. Is BFS good enough?

Show answer

No. BFS returns the route with the fewest moves, and here that is not the fastest. A 5-step route through two narrow aisles takes 11 seconds, while an 8-step route around them takes 8 seconds. When steps have different costs you need UCS — or A*, once you add a heuristic.

UCS knows how much a path has cost so far. But what if we could also estimate how much cost remains to reach the goal?

12 min read

Section 3.5

Informed Search

Greedy Best-First Search and A*

What if the search algorithm could estimate which nodes are more promising?

Informed search uses a heuristic to estimate the remaining cost to the goal and guide which nodes to explore next.

The children's game: "hot and cold"

Looking for a hidden object by opening every drawer in order is uninformed search. Having a friend say "warmer... warmer... cold!" is informed search. Your friend does not tell you where the object is. He only ranks your choices. That ranking is a heuristic.

Heuristic — h(n). A heuristic is an estimate of the remaining cost from a state to the goal. It uses available knowledge to help the search algorithm choose promising nodes. The estimate does not have to be exact.

We write $h(n)$ for the estimated cost of the cheapest path from the state at node $n$ to a goal. At the goal itself, $h = 0$. A heuristic should be cheap to compute. Section 3.6 shows how to check whether an estimate is safe for A*.

بالعربية

الـHeuristic هي دالة تقديرية تساعد خوارزمية البحث على توقع التكلفة المتبقية للوصول إلى الهدف، اعتمادًا على معلومات متاحة عن المشكلة. وهي ليست بالضرورة التكلفة الفعلية.

The heuristic used in this section is the straight-line distance: for maps, the distance in a straight line to the destination. Roads curve, so the real drive is never shorter than this. It fits here because the path cost is also a distance, in kilometres. If the cost were travel time or money, the straight-line distance would not automatically be a safe estimate (section 3.6).

A heuristic is an informed estimate, not a random guess. The straight-line distance is computed from real information about the problem: the positions of the places on the map. A random number would give no reason to prefer one node over another.

How can a search algorithm use $h(n)$? There are two common ways. The first is often quick, but it can return an expensive path. The second is A*.

Greedy best-first search

Rule: take out the frontier node with the lowest $h(n)$ — the one that looks closest to the goal. Greedy search considers only the estimated remaining cost; it ignores the path cost already paid, $g(n)$. Frontier: a priority queue ordered by $h$.

Walking towards a mountain you can see

You always take the path that points most directly at the peak. It works well — until your path meets a deep valley, while the path that curved away had a bridge. Greedy search never looks back at what it spent. It only looks forward at what it hopes is left.

On the delivery map, B looks closest to the customer: its straight-line distance is only 3 km. Greedy search expands B, creates G with $h = 0$, takes G out next, and returns S → B → G: 9 km. The road from B to G is 7 km long, and greedy search never compared this route with the others.

Result: can be fast with a good heuristic, but not optimal. In its tree-like form it is not even complete, because it can bounce between two states that both look good; with a reached table it is complete in a finite state space. Worst case $O(b^m)$.

A*: combining path cost and heuristic

!
First, the name

A* is written with a star and said out loud as "A-star". The star is part of the name — it is not multiplication and not a footnote mark. It comes from the 1968 paper by Hart, Nilsson and Raphael: they called their family of algorithms "A", and marked with a star the version they proved always returns the cheapest path.

Start with one number. In the delivery map, the node for B has $g = 2$: the driver has already driven 2 km. Its $h = 3$: the customer is 3 km away in a straight line. Add the two: $2 + 3 = 5$, so "a route through B will cost at least about 5 km." Both numbers are kilometres, so adding them makes sense. If $g$ were in kilometres and $h$ in minutes, the sum would mean nothing.

A* expands the node with the smallest $f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$, where $g(n)$ is the cost already paid to reach $n$, and $h(n)$ is the estimate of the cost still to pay. So $f(n)$ is an estimate of the total cost of the best solution passing through $n$. Frontier: a priority queue ordered by $f$.

AlgorithmTakes out the frontier node with the lowest
UCS$g(n)$ — cost so far
Greedy best-first$h(n)$ — estimated cost remaining
A*$f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$ — estimated total cost through the node
Three evaluation rules. The algorithms differ only in the number they use to choose the next node from the frontier.
A* connects UCS and Greedy Best-First Search

All three are best-first search. They use different evaluation functions to prioritize nodes in the frontier: uniform-cost search uses $f(n) = g(n)$, greedy best-first search uses $f(n) = h(n)$, and A* uses $f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$ — what has been paid plus what is estimated. So setting $h(n) = 0$ turns A* into UCS, and ignoring $g(n)$ turns it into greedy search. The famous guarantee comes from adding the two: if the estimate is never too high, then $f$ is never too high either, so A* cannot settle for an expensive goal while a cheaper one is still reachable (the exact conditions are below).

Worked example: A* on the delivery map

Remember that A* works on the model, not on the road: it expands nodes on the map, and the driver starts driving only after A* returns a route. Each circle now also shows $h$: the straight-line distance in kilometres from that place to the customer. The table follows A* one step at a time. In every step A* takes out the node with the smallest $f$, tests it, and, if it is not the goal, expands it.

Swipe sideways to see the whole table →

StepTaken outWhat A* doesFrontier after the step, smallest f first
0—Start.S (0 + 5 = 5)
1S, f = 5Creates A, B and D.B (2 + 3 = 5) · A (3 + 4 = 7) · D (3 + 6 = 9)
2B, f = 5Creates C with g = 6, and G with g = 9. G is the goal, but A* tests only the nodes it takes out.A (3 + 4 = 7) · D (3 + 6 = 9) · C (6 + 3 = 9) · G (9 + 0 = 9)
3A, f = 7Reaches C again, now with g = 3 + 2 = 5, less than 6. Updates the reached table and adds the cheaper C.C (5 + 3 = 8) · D (9) · C (9, old) · G (9)
4C, f = 8Reaches G again, now with g = 5 + 3 = 8, less than 9. Updates G.G (8 + 0 = 8) · D (9) · C (9, old) · G (9, old)

When two nodes have the same f, the one that entered the frontier first comes out first. "Old" marks an entry whose state was later reached more cheaply.

Read the table in two directions. The "Taken out" column lists the nodes A* expands, in order: S, B, A, C, then G. Along each row, the last column is the frontier: nodes created but not expanded yet.

Three things to notice:

  1. The goal appeared early

    G entered the frontier at step 2 with $g = 9$. Had A* tested nodes when it created them, it would have returned the 9 km route. Testing when a node is taken out gave the cheaper path through C time to arrive.

  2. Cheaper paths replace dearer ones

    At steps 3 and 4, A* reached C and G again more cheaply. It updated the reached table and added the new nodes. The old entries stay in the frontier; if one ever reaches the front, A* skips it.

  3. The heuristic saved work

    A* never expanded D: $f(D) = 3 + 6 = 9$ is larger than the cost of the solution, 8. Uniform-cost search, which ignores $h$, expands D before C (section 3.4).

Now step through the same search yourself. The table above is the full record; the tracer shows one step at a time on the map.

Admissible: when A* returns the cheapest path

$h(n)$ is admissible if it never overestimates the true remaining cost: $h(n)$ is less than or equal to the real cost of the cheapest path from $n$ to a goal. An admissible heuristic is an optimist: it may think the goal is nearer than it is, but never further.

Not admissible (too pessimistic)

What goes wrong

  • Overestimates the real cost somewhere
  • A* may reject the true best route as "too expensive"
  • You may still get an answer, but not always the cheapest one
  • It can expand fewer nodes, and some systems accept that trade on purpose
Admissible (optimistic)

What you gain

  • Never overestimates the real cost
  • With finite b, step costs of at least ε, and cheaper paths handled correctly (as in the code below), A* returns a cheapest path
  • A higher admissible estimate usually means fewer nodes expanded
  • h(n) = 0 is admissible but gives no help — A* becomes UCS

Consistent: the stronger version

$h$ is consistent if, for every node $n$ and every child $n'$ reached by a step of cost $c$: $h(n) \le c + h(n')$. In words: taking one step should never improve your estimate by more than that step actually cost.

Every consistent heuristic is also admissible. The opposite is not always true. Straight-line distance is consistent: no road from $n$ to $n'$ is shorter than the straight line between them, so $h(n) \le c + h(n')$ always holds. Measured in kilometres, it is also admissible — which is why A* returned the cheapest route on the delivery map.

Optional: why consistency saves work

With a consistent $h$, the first time A* takes a state out of the frontier it has already found the cheapest way there, so it never has to expand that state again. With an $h$ that is admissible but not consistent, the code below still returns a cheapest path, but it may have to expand some states a second time, after it finds a cheaper path to them.

Optional: A* in Python 
import heapq

def a_star(problem, h):
    """A* = best-first search using f(n) = g(n) + h(n)."""
    start = Node(problem.initial)
    frontier = [(h(start.state), 0, start)]   # (f, tie-breaker, node)
    reached = {problem.initial: start}        # best node found for each state
    counter = 0

    while frontier:
        _, _, node = heapq.heappop(frontier)
        if node.path_cost > reached[node.state].path_cost:
            continue                          # old entry: a cheaper path was found later

        if problem.is_goal(node.state):       # test on the way OUT
            return node

        for child in expand(problem, node):
            s = child.state
            # keep the child if it is new, or cheaper than the path we had
            if s not in reached or child.path_cost < reached[s].path_cost:
                reached[s] = child
                counter += 1
                f = child.path_cost + h(s)
                heapq.heappush(frontier, (f, counter, child))
    return None                               # frontier empty: no solution

Four details make this code correct. The counter breaks ties in $f$: the node pushed first comes out first, which is the rule used in the table. The first check skips old entries, so a state is never expanded through a path that is already known to be too expensive. The goal test comes after the node is taken out, not when it is created. And the returned node carries its parent links, so path(node) from section 3.2 rebuilds the route. Run on the delivery map with the straight-line $h$, it returns the node for G with path_cost 8, and path gives the actions to A, to C, to G.

What A* guarantees

✅ Complete

When the branching factor is finite and every step costs at least some fixed amount ε > 0.

🏆 Optimal

Under the same conditions, with an admissible h, as long as A* puts a state back in the frontier when it finds a cheaper path to it (the code above does). With a consistent h, it never has to expand a state twice.

💾 Hungry for memory

A* keeps the frontier and the reached table in memory — in the worst case, every state it has reached. A good heuristic reduces how many that is, but the number can still grow exponentially with depth, so on hard problems memory usually runs out before time.

Check yourself

A real map. Road numbers are driving distances in kilometres; the number in each circle is $h$, the straight-line distance to Riyadh. Which route does greedy best-first search return, and which does A* return? For A*, compute $f$ for the first two choices out of Makkah.

Road distances are approximate. Straight-line values were computed from city coordinates.
Show answer

Greedy looks only at $h$. Madinah (714) really is closer to Riyadh in a straight line than Taif (746), so greedy goes north: Makkah → Madinah → Buraydah → Riyadh, 1460 km.

A* adds what it already paid. Through Taif: $g = 90$, $h = 746$, so $f = 836$. Through Madinah: $g = 450$, $h = 714$, so $f = 1164$. A* expands Taif first, then Afif ($g = 510$, $f = 510 + 391 = 901$), and creates Riyadh with $g = f = 940$. Riyadh comes out before Madinah (1164), so A* returns Makkah → Taif → Afif → Riyadh, 940 km, without ever expanding Madinah.

14 min read

Section 3.6

Evaluating Heuristics

Is the Estimate Safe?

The heuristic affects how efficiently A* searches. An admissible heuristic helps A* guarantee an optimal solution under the appropriate conditions. When $h(n) = 0$, A* behaves like UCS. A more informative admissible heuristic can often reduce the number of nodes explored.

This section has one central question: is the estimate safe? In other words, is the heuristic admissible? Comparing two heuristics and designing new ones are further exploration, at the end of the section.

Is this h too high? Check it against the real cost

Admissibility is a promise about every node: $h(n)$ is never larger than the real cost of the cheapest path from $n$ to a goal. On a small map you can check the promise by hand. Here are the straight-line values from the delivery map, next to the real remaining cost of the cheapest road route:

Placeh(n)Real remaining costToo high?
S58 (S → A → C → G)No
A45 (A → C → G)No
B37 (B → G, or B → C → G)No
C33 (C → G)No — equal is allowed
D611 (D → S, then 8 more)No
Every value is at or below the real cost, so this h is admissible.

This check works because $h$ and the real cost use the same unit: kilometres of driving distance. The straight-line distance is never longer than the driving distance, so it is safe for this cost. A heuristic that is safe for one cost measure is not necessarily safe for another, such as travel time (see the Check yourself below).

Now suppose someone sets $h(B) = 8$, because "B's road to the customer is long". The real remaining cost from B is 7, and 8 is larger: this $h$ is not admissible. On this map the damage happens to be invisible, because the best route avoids B anyway. But the guarantee is gone: on another map, an estimate that is too high can hide the best route.

i
Further exploration: dominance and designing heuristics (not in the quiz)

The examples use the 8-puzzle (the further exploration box in section 3.1) and two heuristics for it:

  • h₁ — misplaced tiles: count the tiles that are not in their correct square. Each one needs at least one move.
  • h₂ — Manhattan distance: for every tile, add its horizontal and vertical distance from its correct square. Each tile needs at least that many moves.

Dominance: comparing two admissible heuristics. If both are admissible and $h_2(n) \ge h_1(n)$ for every node, we say $h_2$ dominates $h_1$. That is the whole definition: a statement about the two functions. $h_2$ is never smaller, and never too high.

What it usually means for A*. A larger admissible estimate is closer to the real remaining cost, so it tends to steer A* more directly towards the goal and to expand fewer nodes.

When it becomes a guarantee. If both heuristics are also consistent — as $h_1$ and $h_2$ are — and A* runs the same way with each, every node that A* expands with $h_2$ is also expanded with $h_1$, except possibly some nodes whose $f$ equals the cost of the best solution, where the order of ties decides. So A* with $h_2$ expands no more nodes than with $h_1$, apart from ties. Even then it is a guarantee about nodes, not about seconds: $h_2$ may cost more to compute at each node.

How large is the difference in practice? Russell & Norvig (3rd edition) report averages over 100 random 8-puzzle problems that need 12 moves: iterative deepening, with no heuristic, created about 3.6 million nodes; A* with $h_1$ about 230; A* with $h_2$ about 70. Your own counts will differ with the implementation and the tie-breaking rule.

Where do heuristics come from? Three common ways:

  1. Relax the problem: remove a rule. A relaxed problem is the same problem with fewer rules, so it is easier to solve exactly. If a tile could jump anywhere, the exact cost is the number of misplaced tiles — that is $h_1$. If a tile could slide onto any neighbouring square, even a full one, the exact cost is the Manhattan distance — that is $h_2$. The exact cost of a relaxed problem is always an admissible heuristic for the real one, because every real solution is also a solution of the relaxed problem.
  2. Solve part of the problem exactly. Compute in advance the exact cost of putting tiles 1 to 4 in place, ignoring the others, and save it in a table. Then just look it up during the search.
  3. Take the largest of several. If $h_a$ and $h_b$ are both admissible, then $\max(h_a, h_b)$ is admissible too, and it dominates both. You pay to compute both, so do this only when each one is cheap.
!
Accuracy against computation cost

A perfect heuristic would walk you straight to the goal — but computing it exactly means solving the problem first, so you gained nothing. The real engineering question is the balance: is this estimate accurate enough to be worth its cost at every node?

i
Further exploration: learned heuristics (not in the quiz)

Some modern systems learn $h$ from data: a model is trained on problems that were already solved, and it predicts the remaining cost of new states. A learned estimate can be sharp, but nothing forces it to stay at or below the real cost. It is not automatically admissible, so A*'s guarantee of a cheapest path does not come with it.

Check yourself

On a road map, is straight-line distance admissible when the cost is kilometres? What if the cost is travel time?

Show answer

In kilometres: yes. No road is shorter than the straight line. In travel time: not automatically. You must divide the distance by the highest possible speed on the network. If you divide by an average speed instead, you will overestimate on fast highways, break admissibility, and lose the A* guarantee. Units matter.

7 min read

Section 3.7

Applications of Search

Search is not only a classroom exercise. It is part of services you use every week.

Where and why search is used

In each example below, an agent must choose a sequence of actions or decisions from many possibilities. Trying them in a model first is cheaper and safer than trying them in the real world.

🧭 Route planning

Maps apps find routes over road graphs with millions of edges, using improved versions of Dijkstra's algorithm and A*, and plan again when traffic changes.

🚚 Delivery services

Delivery apps in Saudi cities decide which driver takes which order, and in which order to visit the stops: a search over possible routes and orders.

📅 Scheduling

Assigning exams to rooms and time slots at a university is a search through a huge space of possible timetables.

🤖 Warehouse robots

Robots in large warehouses search for a path to the shelf they need that avoids collisions with shelves and with other robots.

🕋 Crowd routing in Hajj and Umrah

Planning safe walking routes and gate assignments for very large crowds is a search over paths with capacity limits.

🧠 Assistants that plan their own steps

What industry calls agentic AI (Module 2) are systems that pursue a goal with little step-by-step human direction — and choosing their sequence of steps is a search problem.

Search is also used to improve AI systems themselves. When we build a machine learning model, we choose settings such as its learning rate (you will meet it in Module 4) or how many layers it has. A simple way is to try several settings, train a model with each one, and keep the one that scores best on data the model did not train on. Here the path does not matter, only the best setting does — the kind of optimization that Module 4 studies (section 4.4).

Choosing a search strategy

How do we decide between BFS, DFS, UCS, greedy best-first search, and A*? Three questions decide most choices in this module: do all steps cost the same, is memory tight, and do you have a good heuristic?

Your situationChooseWhy
All steps cost the same, enough memoryBFSFewest steps is then the cheapest path.
Memory is very tight, any solution will do, the state space is finite and not too deepDFSNeeds little memory; no guarantee of a cheapest path.
Steps have different costs, no heuristicUCSTakes out the lowest path cost first.
Steps have different costs, an admissible heuristic existsA*Still a cheapest path; with a consistent h it never expands more nodes than UCS, apart from ties.
Any path will do, quickly, and a heuristic existsGreedy best-firstFollows h only: fast, but with no guarantee of a cheapest path.
There is no "best" search algorithm. There is only the best fit for the costs, the memory, and the knowledge you have.

Further exploration: when all steps cost the same and memory is tight, iterative deepening (the box in section 3.4) offers the guarantees of BFS with the memory of DFS.

The whole module in three steps

  1. Model the problem

    Describe it with five parts: initial state, actions, transition model, goal test, and action cost. Keep only the details that change the answer. A clear formulation is most of the work.

  2. Explain the strategy

    A search algorithm grows a tree from a frontier and remembers the states it has reached. What makes each algorithm different is how it chooses the next node: BFS the shallowest, DFS the deepest, UCS the lowest $g$, greedy search the lowest $h$, and A* the lowest $g + h$. Judge each one on completeness, optimality, time, and memory — and expect memory to be the limit that stops you.

  3. Experiment and compare

    Trace the algorithms on a small problem, count the nodes they expand, and compare the paths they return. Then choose by what you have: equal or different step costs, enough memory or not, and a heuristic or none. With an admissible heuristic, a finite branching factor, and every step costing at least some ε > 0, A* returns a cheapest path, usually after far fewer nodes than UCS.

Check yourself

You are assigning 400 exams to rooms and time slots at the university. No student may have two exams at the same time, and you would like as few students as possible to have two exams on the same day. Write the five parts if you build the timetable one exam at a time. Then ask: does the order in which you placed the exams matter to anyone?

Show answer

As a path search. States: partial timetables (some exams placed, some not). Actions: place the next exam in a legal room and slot. Transition model: the timetable with that exam added. Goal test: all exams placed and no hard requirement broken. Action cost: what each placement adds to the thing to improve (Module 2) — for example, one point for each student who now has two exams on the same day.

With that cost, the path cost is the score of the finished timetable, and UCS or A* would find a cheapest sequence of placements. That is already optimization: path search can aim at the best answer too.

But the order does not matter to anyone. Students see only the final timetable. When only the final result counts, we can stop building paths and work directly with complete timetables, improving them one change at a time.

i
Further exploration: AI search and search engines (not in the quiz)

The word search has a second meaning in computing. This module searches for a sequence of actions that reaches a goal. A search engine performs information retrieval: it looks for documents that are relevant to a query.

  • Input. AI search: a problem — initial state, actions, goal. Information retrieval: a query — words or a question.
  • Output. AI search: a path, that is, a sequence of actions. Information retrieval: a ranked list of documents.
  • Judged by. AI search: reaching the goal, and the path cost. Information retrieval: how relevant the top results are.
  • Example. AI search: S → A → C → G, 8 km. Information retrieval: the university pages about exam rules.

Semantic search ranks documents by meaning rather than by exact words, by comparing number vectors (embeddings) of the query and of each document. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) joins retrieval and text generation: a retrieval step finds relevant passages, and a large language model writes an answer from them. Neither plans a sequence of actions, so neither is the search of this module.

Where this takes you next

Sometimes we need a sequence of actions to reach a goal. Other times, we mainly care about finding a good solution, not the path used to discover it. That second case opens Module 4, Optimization — Finding Better Solutions. Local search improves candidate solutions instead of finding paths to a goal, so it usually does not keep the path that led to an answer.

The later modules reuse this module too. Adversarial search (Module 5) searches a tree where an opponent chooses every second move, and constraint satisfaction (Module 6) searches partial assignments, like the timetable above.

Revision card

Module 3 cheat sheet

The five parts of a search problem

  • Initial state — where the agent starts
  • Actions — what it can do in a state
  • Transition model — where each action leads
  • Goal test — how to know you are done
  • Action cost — the price of one step; add them for the path cost
  • Solution = any path from start to goal · optimal solution = a cheapest one
  • A heuristic is not one of the five parts: it is extra knowledge for the solver

Three numbers not to mix

  • Path cost — the cost of the answer (the 8 km the driver drives)
  • Search time — the algorithm's work: nodes created or expanded
  • Search memory — what it stores at once: frontier and reached table

Key formulas

  • g(n) = cost already paid from the start to n
  • h(n) = estimated cost from n to the goal, in the same unit as g
  • f(n) = g(n) + h(n) — this is A*
  • h(n) = 0 → A* becomes UCS
  • ignore g(n) → A* becomes greedy search
  • Admissible: h(n) ≤ real remaining cost
  • Consistent: h(n) ≤ c + h(n')

Which algorithm, when

  • Equal step costs, enough memory → BFS
  • Very tight memory, any solution, finite and shallow space → DFS (no guarantee)
  • Different step costs, no heuristic → UCS
  • Admissible heuristic, need a cheapest path → A*
  • Any path, quickly, with a heuristic → greedy best-first (no guarantee)

Complexity table

  • BFS — queue; complete if b is finite; optimal if equal costs; time and memory O(b^d)
  • DFS — stack; tree-like: not complete, not optimal; time O(b^m), memory O(bm)
  • UCS — priority queue by g; complete and optimal if b is finite and every step costs at least ε > 0

A* on the delivery map

  • Takes out S (f 5), B (f 5), A (f 7), C (f 8), then G (f 8)
  • G is created at step 2 with g = 9, but is not returned: the goal is tested when taken out
  • C and G are reached again more cheaply; the old entries are skipped
  • D is never expanded: f(D) = 9 is more than the solution cost, 8
  • Answer: S → A → C → G, 8 km. Greedy and BFS both return S → B → G, 9 km

Mistakes that cost marks

  • Saying BFS is always optimal — it is guaranteed only when all steps cost the same
  • Calling the driving distance the search time — path cost belongs to the answer, search time to the algorithm
  • Testing the goal when a node is created in UCS or A* instead of when it is taken out
  • Confusing a state with a node: one state can appear in many nodes
  • Confusing the frontier (nodes waiting to be expanded) with the reached table (states already reached)
  • Giving O(bm) memory to a DFS that keeps a reached table of every state
  • Adding g in kilometres to h in minutes — g and h must use the same unit
  • Forgetting the reached table and then wondering why the search never stops
  • Thinking the agent moves while it searches — it searches its model first, and only then acts

Further exploration — not in the quiz (optional)

  • Dominance: both admissible and h₂(n) ≥ h₁(n) for every n → A* with h₂ usually expands fewer nodes
  • DLS — DFS that never goes deeper than a limit ℓ
  • IDS — DLS with ℓ = 0, 1, 2, …: the guarantees of BFS with the memory of DFS, when steps cost the same and memory is tight
